R's most-used data structures are vectors, matrices, arrays, lists, factors,
and data frames. This chapter covers the first two.

# Scalars and Vectors (1D)

A scalar is any single number; a vector is a collection of values of the
same type (and can represent a sequence).

Mixing types inside `c()` forces R to coerce everything to one common type:
```{r}
v <- c(1, "R", TRUE, FALSE, NA)
print(v)
class(v) # everything becomes character (NA is compatible with any type)
```

```{r}
v2 <- c(1, 4, 8, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, "R" == "r")
print(v2)
class(v2) # everything becomes numeric: FALSE -> 0, TRUE -> 1
```

## Sequences with `seq()`
```{r}
x <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 90)
length(x)
unique(round(diff(x), 5)) # the common step size

head(x, 5); tail(x)
range(x)
```

```{r}
diff(c(4, 6))
diff(range(x)) # same as max(x) - min(x)
```

Indexing with a non-integer floors to the nearest integer:
```{r}
x[11.8] == x[11]
as.integer(9.123486785) # what R does internally with a fractional index
```

The length of a vector:
```{r}
length(x)
a <- 9
length(a) # a scalar is just a vector of length 1
```

## Repetition with `rep()`
```{r}
rep("I learn R", 3)
rep(c(0, 1), 5)
rep(c(0:1), c(3, 3))
rep(c(0:1), each = 3)
```

## Random sampling
```{r}
set.seed(123) # fixes the randomness for reproducibility
y <- sample(0:1, size = 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(1/3, 1 - 1/3))
sum(y == 0)   # count of zeros
sum(y == 1)   # count of ones
```

`table()` counts occurrences for you:
```{r}
table(y)
```

`prop.table()` converts counts to proportions:
```{r}
prop.table(table(y))
mean(y == 0) # a shortcut: mean() of a logical vector is a proportion
```

## A small survey example

```{r}
Gender <- c("Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", "Female", "Female", "Male",
"Male", "Female", "Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", "Male", "Female",
"Female", "Male", "Female", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Male",
"Male", "Male", "Male", "Female", "Femaale", "Male", "Female",
"Male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "Female", "Malle", "Male", "Female",
"Female", "Femmale", "Female", "Female", "Female", "Female", "Male",
"Male", "Male", "Male")

sum(Gender == "Female")
mean(Gender == "Female")
table(Gender) # note the 3 misspelled entries
```

Cleaning up the typos:
```{r}
Gender[Gender == "Femaale"] <- "Female"
Gender[Gender == "Femmale"] <- "Female"
Gender[Gender == "Malle"]   <- "Male"
table(Gender)
```

Sub-setting with `sample()`:
```{r}
set.seed(76)
table(sample(Gender, size = 20))
```

## Vector arithmetic
```{r}
k <- 2
v <- c(1, 0, 3)

k + v; v + k
k - v; v - k
k * v; v * k
v / k
k / v
```

```{r}
k <- 1/2
v <- c(pi, 0, 1, 4)
w <- c(0, pi, pi, 0, 0)

k * v; v * k
v ^ k
v + w
```

# Matrices (2D)

```{r}
(A <- matrix(1:25, ncol = 5, nrow = 5)) # column-major fill by default
(B <- matrix(1:25, nrow = 5, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE))
```

## Building a matrix by hand
```{r}
v <- c(1, rep(0, 2), 1, 0, rep(1, 3), rep(0, 2), rep(1, 2))
A <- matrix(v, 3, byrow = TRUE)
print(A)
dim(A)
```

The same result using `dim<-`:
```{r}
v <- c(1, rep(0, 2), 1, 0, rep(1, 3), rep(0, 2), rep(1, 2))
dim(v) <- c(4, 3)
v <- t(v)
v
```

A zero matrix:
```{r}
n <- 6; p <- 8
matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = p)
```

```{r}
(A <- matrix(c(1, 0, 2, 5, 2, 1, 4, 2, 0), nrow = 3))
(B <- matrix(c(2, 5, 2, 3, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1), nrow = 3))
```

## Matrices from vectors: `cbind` / `rbind`
```{r}
v1 <- c(1, 0, 2); v2 <- c(5, 2, 1); v3 <- c(4, 2, 0)
(M1 <- cbind(v1, v2, v3))
(M2 <- rbind(v1, v2, v3))
```

## Matrix operations

Transpose:
```{r}
(A_T <- t(A))
```

Addition / subtraction:
```{r}
A + B
A - B
```

Multiplication (`%*%`, not `*`):
```{r}
ncol(A) == nrow(B)
A %*% B
```

Inverse:
```{r}
(A_inv <- solve(A))
round(A %*% A_inv) # sanity check: should be the identity matrix
```

## Solving a system of equations

$$
\begin{cases}
2x + 2y &= 0\\
x + 3y &= 2
\end{cases}
$$

```{r}
A1 <- matrix(c(2, 2, 1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(0, 2)
solve(A1, b)
```

## Eigenvalues / eigenvectors

Eigenvalues $\lambda$ of a square matrix $A$ solve the characteristic
equation $\det(A - \lambda I_n) = 0$. They're the mathematical basis of
[Principal Component Analysis](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/pca-analysis-r),
covered in Chapter 15.

```{r}
ev <- eigen(A)
print(ev$values)

P <- ev$vectors
round(solve(P) %*% A %*% P, 4) # recovers a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues
```

## Worked exercise: manual PCA on `iris`

1. Remove the last column (`Species`) from `iris`:
```{r}
data(iris)
dta <- iris[, -5]
```

2. Compute the average of each remaining column:
```{r}
avg <- colMeans(dta)
print(avg)
```

3. Center the data by subtracting each column's average:
```{r}
scaled_dta <- scale(dta, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
head(scaled_dta, 3)
```

4. Eigen-decompose `t(scaled_dta) %*% scaled_dta`:
```{r}
cov_mat <- t(scaled_dta) %*% scaled_dta
ev <- eigen(cov_mat)
ev$values
```

5. Project onto the first two eigenvectors:
```{r}
P <- ev$vectors[, 1:2]
projection <- scaled_dta %*% P
head(projection)
```

This is exactly what `prcomp()` does under the hood:
```{r}
pca <- prcomp(dta, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
head(pca$x[, 1:2])
```
